events.title: Turing publishes Computing Machinery and Intelligence
events.summary: Alan [Turing]'s October 1950 Mind paper asked whether machines can think and proposed the [imitation game] — now called the [Turing test].
events.about: [Turing] reframed intelligence as behavior observable over a [teletype] conversation, not inner experience. The paper anticipated [machine learning] objections, consciousness debates, and every chatbot [benchmark] that followed — from ELIZA to modern [LLM] evals.

narrative.whyChosen: This is the founding document of philosophy-of-AI and practical [machine intelligence] testing.
narrative.whyImportant: It gave researchers a concrete experiment instead of endless definitions of 'thinking.'
narrative.problemSolved: There was no operational way to discuss [machine intelligence] without metaphysics.

events.title: Turing: "Can machines think?"
events.quoteText: I propose to consider the question, 'Can machines think?'
events.summary: [Turing] opens his 1950 Mind paper by reframing the question of [machine intelligence] — leading to the [imitation game] thought experiment.
events.about: Instead of defining 'think,' [Turing] proposed a conversational test: if a machine's answers are indistinguishable from a human's, the question of thinking becomes less important than observable capability. The opening line launched seventy years of AI debate.

narrative.whyChosen: The opening sentence of the most cited paper in AI philosophy.
narrative.whyImportant: It shifted the debate from consciousness to measurable behavior.
narrative.problemSolved: Philosophers could not agree what 'thinking' meant for humans, let alone machines.
